summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a free web tool that lets mission planners, teachers and the public compare Moon landing sites and dates in seconds. Pick one of 24 official sites from NASA Moon Trek (Artemis III regions, CLPS missions, ISRO, JAXA, Apollo 11) or click anywhere on the south pole map, then choose a date. The tool shows the Sun and Earth against the real LOLA terrain horizon and answers two questions: will the lander have solar power, and can it talk directly to Earth? It shows how long each will last, finds landing windows, compares sites side by side, and maps better spots within 15 km. This matters because at the south pole the Sun skims the horizon, so a few kilometres or a few days can decide a mission, and launch delays force fast replanning. All results come from NASA JPL Horizons, LRO LOLA, Moon Trek and LROC QuickMap data, validated against Moon Trek's shadow map (98.7% agreement). For everyone else, an Astronaut View lets you walk on real lunar terrain, see which cities can see the Moon, and hunt for Jade Rabbits from the Chang'e legend.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Landing Site Navigator answers two questions for any lunar landing site and date: will the lander have sunlight for solar power, and can it talk directly to Earth? The website has six tabs that share one sidebar, where you choose the site and date.

- Plan a landing: choose one of 24 official sites from NASA Moon Trek (13 Artemis III candidate regions, 7 CLPS missions, ISRO Chandrayaan-3, JAXA SLIM, Apollo 11, Shackleton crater floor), or click anywhere on the south pole map; the terrain horizon for a custom site is computed live in the browser. A sky panorama shows the real terrain horizon with the Sun and Earth at their true angular size and their paths for the next 30 days. A verdict (GO / NO COMMS / NO POWER) shows the Sun and Earth elevation, time until sunset or Earthset, the longest darkness and solar-panel output. A 30-day timeline and a seasonal overview of every lunar day from 2026 to 2028 show how conditions change. You can compare all sites side by side on one date, and a landing-window finder lists the dates when the Sun and Earth are both in view for N or more days.

- Nearby spots: a heatmap of the share of time sunlit, Earth-visible and both, for 3,721 points on a 0.5 km grid within 15 km. Example: the Connecting Ridge region centre is sunlit 48% of the time, but a spot 10 km south is sunlit 79%. Click a cell to move the site there.

- Walk on the Moon: 3D NASA LOLA terrain out to 150 km, lit by the real Sun. In the Astronaut View you stand 2 m above the ground and walk with the keyboard; at every step the tool checks against the terrain whether the Sun and Earth are visible from where you stand.

- See Earth: the face of Earth seen from the site, with day and night, time zones and Earth's phase; which world cities can see the Moon right now; and which NASA Deep Space Network antenna can talk to the lander.

- Chang'e & Jade Rabbit: Chang'e's flight calculator uses the real Earth-Moon distance for the chosen date (walking 9.1 years, Taiwan High Speed Rail 55.2 days, Apollo 11 3.1 days, light 1.32 seconds), plus why it is not that simple: the Moon moves at 3,680 km/h, escape speed is 11 km/s, and the distance changes from 356,648 to 406,603 km. In a game, players walk on the real terrain to find five Jade Rabbits; three of them hide in the darkest, coldest spots, where water ice can survive.

- Learn why: why the polar Sun is so low, why a few kilometres matter, libration, the 29.5-day lunar day, shadows without air, and the Canadian Space Agency's lunar rover.

- Each site also lists its LROC NAC images (from LROC QuickMap) and offers a one-click query in JPL Horizons to verify the result.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline downloads hourly sub-solar, sub-Earth and sub-Moon points from the NASA JPL Horizons API for November 2026 to December 2028 (19,009 hourly steps). It computes the terrain horizon in 720 directions for each site from LRO LOLA topography (80 m and 240 m grids), including the curvature of the Moon. The Moon has no atmosphere, so no refraction correction is applied. Libration and the changing Earth-Moon distance come directly from the Horizons ephemeris. The web app then computes the Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation for any site and hour in the browser and compares them with the horizon.

Validation: our Sun and Earth positions match direct Horizons topocentric queries to better than 0.01 degrees. Our sunlight model agrees with NASA Moon Trek's LOLA permanently-shadowed-regions map at 98.7% of 300 random south-pole points (149/150 shadowed and 147/150 sunlit points correctly identified).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Mission planners: when a launch slips or hardware changes, see in seconds which nearby sites and dates still give power and communications, instead of working through several expert tools.

- Science and engineering teams: one shared visual answer to "power and comms?"

- Rover teams, such as the Canadian Space Agency's lunar rover: see how far to drive for better sunlight.

- Students and the public: feel why the lunar south pole is so hard, and so exciting. The tool is free, runs in any browser and needs no installation or login.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

The same NASA data serves two audiences. Planners get numbers and comparisons; everyone else can stand on the landing site as an astronaut, look back at Earth and see which cities can see the Moon right now. The Chang'e and Jade Rabbit legend, which people across Asia know, turns the Earth-Moon distance and the Moon's permanent shadows into a story and a game: the rabbits hide exactly where our sunlight map finds the darkest, coldest ground.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Real topography instead of a flat horizon; no atmosphere (no refraction); the curvature of the Moon; Earth's libration and the Moon's changing distance; steep slopes and deep craters at the south pole; time remaining before sunset and Earthset; fast comparison of many site-date scenarios; and ease of use for non-experts (plain-language verdicts, guided tabs, and a Learn tab).

TOOLS

Python (numpy, Pillow), JavaScript, HTML/CSS, Canvas, three.js, d3, Git and GitHub Pages. AI coding assistant: Claude (Anthropic).
dataRefs: NASA JPL Horizons System (API): hourly Sun and Earth geometry for the Moon, 2026-2028
NASA Moon Trek: Artemis III Candidate Landing Regions and LOLA Permanently Shadowed Regions map (validation)
NASA Moon Trek: CLPS Landing Sites layer
LROC QuickMap: LRO NAC image coverage for each site
LRO LOLA Gridded Topography (LDEM_80S_80M, LDEM_75S_240M), NASA Planetary Data System
NASA JPL Horizons API (used by the data pipeline)
projectRefs: CSA (Canadian Space Agency) Moon Exploration: lunar rover and Artemis II content in the Learn tab
ISRO Chandrayaan-3: landing site used as a comparison site
JAXA SLIM: landing site used as a comparison site
Natural Earth 1:110m land (public domain): Earth coastlines on the globe
world-atlas (ISC licence): Natural Earth land data package
three.js r128 with OrbitControls (MIT licence): 3D terrain view
Python with numpy and Pillow: data pipeline
Claude (Anthropic): AI coding and writing assistant
